Data science extracts knowledge from data. Over 28 lessons this course walks the whole
process once, end to end — acquiring data, exploring it, mining it for structure,
visualizing what you find, building two case-study systems on it, and reckoning with what
you owe the people the data came from.

Everything here runs. Every number, table, and figure on these pages was produced by
executing the code you see next to it.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Start here

New to the course? Read [What Is Data Science? The Process and the
Landscape](u01_introduction/l01_concept_intro_data_science.qmd), then work through [Lab:
The Data Scientist's Toolkit](u01_introduction/l02_lab_data_science_toolkit.md) — it gets
you running code in the browser within minutes, with nothing to install.
:::

## How the course works

Each lesson comes in one or two parts, and units end with something you build:

- **Concept notes** introduce an idea, with worked examples and the reasoning behind the
  technique. Start here for each lesson.
- **Labs** are runnable notebooks. You open them in Google Colab and execute them
  yourself; every lab is paired with its concept note.
- **Mini-projects** close Units III, IV, and VI. These are not new material — they hand
  you a messy question and make you choose among the techniques the unit taught, then
  defend the choice.

A short retrieval quiz opens most sessions, covering the previous lesson. It is low-stakes
and its purpose is to help the material stick, not to rank you.

## Course coverage

| Unit | Lessons | What you will do |
|------|---------|------------------|
| [I — Introduction](u01_introduction/l01_concept_intro_data_science.qmd) | L01–L02 | The data-science process and where the field sits; NumPy and pandas on a first messy table |
| [II — Big Data](u02_big_data/l03_concept_big_data_challenges.qmd) | L03–L06 | CSV versus Parquet on a million rows; MapReduce by hand, then PySpark; SQL and NoSQL on one ragged catalogue; pulling live data from a web API |
| [III — Exploratory Data Analysis](u03_eda/l07_concept_eda_intro.qmd) | L07–L10 | Distributions, summary statistics, and a catalogue of charts — closing with a **mini-project** on what drives house prices |
| [IV — Data Mining](u04_data_mining/l11_concept_feature_engineering.qmd) | L11–L15 | Features from raw and from text data; filter-based selection; decision trees and random forests — closing with a **mini-project** on what predicts higher income |
| [V — Visualization](u05_visualization/l16_concept_spatial_visualization.qmd) | L16–L17, L19–L21 | Mapping Puerto Rico earthquakes; 65 years of San Juan climate; correlation and its blind spots; PCA; finding groups and outliers |
| [Foundations — Linear Algebra](foundations/l18_concept_linear_algebra.qmd) | L18 | Vectors, dot products, and projection — the machinery behind correlation, PCA, and recommenders. Taught between L17 and L19 |
| [VI — Recommender Systems](u06_recommender_systems/l22_concept_collaborative_filtering.qmd) | L22–L24 | Collaborative, content-based, and hybrid recommenders on MovieLens; how to evaluate them — closing with a **mini-project** on which one you would ship |
| [VII — Social Networks](u07_social_networks/l25_concept_social_networks_graphs.qmd) | L25–L26 | Relationships as graphs; adjacency matrices and centrality; detecting communities |
| [VIII — Governance](u08_governance/l27_concept_data_ethics.qmd) | L27–L28 | Data ethics through documented cases; GDPR, HIPAA, FERPA, and Puerto Rico law |

## Running the labs

Labs are Jupyter notebooks designed to run in **Google Colab** — free, in the browser,
nothing to install. Every lab page carries an *Open in Colab* badge at the top; click it
and the notebook opens ready to run.

A few things worth knowing:

- **Run the setup cells first.** Each lab opens with two of them: one installs the
  libraries, one imports them and loads the data. Colab resets between sessions, so run
  them every time you open a lab.
- **Save your own copy.** Clicking the badge opens a read-only view of the course
  notebook. Use *File · Save a copy in Drive* before you start working, or your edits are
  lost when you close the tab.
- **The data comes with the lab.** Datasets are bundled in the repository, with a live
  download as fallback, so labs work without hunting for files.
- **The lab pages on this site are read-only.** They show the code together with the
  output it actually produced — useful for reading and review, but you learn this by
  running it yourself.

## What you will be able to do

By the end of the course you should be able to:

1. Describe what data science is, where it is applied, and how the steps of its process
   fit together.
2. Identify the challenges of large-scale data, and use Spark, SQL, NoSQL stores, and web
   APIs to acquire and process it.
3. Explore an unfamiliar dataset — choose the right chart, compute descriptive statistics,
   and say what the two together reveal.
4. Build features from raw and unstructured data, and use filters, decision trees, and
   random forests to find what matters in them.
5. Visualize spatial patterns, temporal patterns, relationships between variables, and
   many variables at once; reduce dimensionality; detect outliers.
6. Build and evaluate a recommender system, and analyze relationships between people as a
   graph.
7. Discuss the ethical, social, legal, and political stakes of data analytics, and cite
   the laws and standards that govern data handling.

## How you are assessed

| | |
|---|---|
| **Retrieval quizzes** | Short multiple-choice, at the start of most sessions, on the previous lesson |
| **Mini-projects** | Three applied deliverables, closing Units III, IV, and VI |
| **Partial exams** | Exam I after Unit IV; Exam II after Unit VIII |
| **Final exam** | Cumulative, during finals week |
| **Final project** | An end-to-end data-science deliverable, assigned around week 9, presented during finals week |

Relative weights are discussed and agreed on the first day of class.
